To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
TLR7 recognition is important for the induction of protective immunological memory in response to the 2007-2009 pandemic split vaccine, but dispensable for influenza virus A infection.
TLR7 recognition is dispensable for influenza virus infection but important for the induction of hemagglutinin-specific antibodies in response to the 2008 pandemic split vaccine in mice.
TLR7 signaling is dispensable for influenza virus infection but is required for induction of humoral responses to influenza virus vaccines.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of Tlr7 in the induction and maintenance of influenza virus-specific humoral immunity.
the development of a novel approach to the study of the role of TRL7 in the development of a vaccine.
the development of a vaccine against influenza virus infection.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

TLR7 is not essential for the induction of protective immune responses to influenza infection, but is required for the induction of long-lasting protective immunity against the 2009 influenza A pandemic split vaccine.
TLR7 is dispensable for the control of influenza virus infection but plays an important role for vaccine-induced humoral immunity.

the absence of Tlr7/Myd88 signaling during influenza virus infection does not impair the induction of protective antibodies but that it is essential for the development of protective immunological memory in response to the 2008 pandemic split vaccine.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the absence of Tlr7 signaling does not affect influenza virus replication, but it does affect the production of virus-specific antibodies and the development of immunological memory in response to vaccination with the 20009 pandemic split vaccine.
TLR7 is not essential for the induction of adaptive immune response to influenza virus infection.
TLR7 is dispensable for influenza virus infection, but it is important for the induction of hemagglutinin-specific antibodies in response to the 2008-09 pandemic inactivated split virus vaccine.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the TLR7 agonist, R848, should be added to the split vaccine to enhance vaccine immunogenicity and to ensure protective efficacy against influenza virus.
the TLR7/8 agonist, resiquimod, is a potent adjuvant for influenza virus vaccines and that the adjuvant effect of resiquimod is likely due to T cell activation.
TLR7 signaling is important in the induction of long-term immunological memory following influenza vaccination.
